## Statement of Need

In [City, State], an estimated [X]% of adults — roughly [NUMBER] residents — lack the literacy skills needed to read a prescription label, complete a job application, or help a child with homework `[CITE #1]`. Low adult literacy is not a fringe issue in our community; it is a quiet barrier that shapes whether a parent can advocate at a school conference, whether a job seeker can move from a $[X]/hour role to a family-sustaining wage, and whether a patient can safely manage a chronic condition. Despite its scale, adult literacy remains one of the most under-resourced areas of workforce and family support in [County].

The numbers tell a consistent story. According to [CITE #1], [X]% of adults in [City] perform at or below Level 1 on national literacy assessments, compared with [Y]% statewide and [Z]% nationally. In the [City School District] service area, [NUMBER] adults ages 18 and older have not completed high school `[CITE #2]`, and the [State] Adult Education office reports that only [X]% of eligible adults in [County] are currently enrolled in any literacy, GED, or English language program `[CITE #3]`. Among residents our organization served last year, [X]% read below a 6th-grade level at intake, and [Y]% were parents of children under 18 — meaning low literacy in our city is also a two-generation issue.

The problem is persistent and, by several measures, worsening. Between [YEAR] and [YEAR], the number of [County] adults without a high school credential rose by [X]%, even as the regional economy shifted toward jobs requiring post-secondary skills `[CITE #2]`. The [Regional Workforce Board]'s most recent labor market analysis projects that [X]% of job openings in [City] over the next five years will require literacy skills at or above Level 2, a threshold that roughly [NUMBER] of our neighbors cannot currently meet. National research reinforces what we see locally: adults with low literacy are [X] times more likely to live in poverty and [Y] times more likely to report poor health outcomes than peers with stronger skills.

Current services cannot meet the need. The [City] public library system, [Community College] adult basic education program, and our organization are the three primary providers of free adult literacy instruction in [County], with a combined capacity of roughly [NUMBER] learners per year — serving fewer than [X]% of eligible adults. Our own waitlist currently stands at [NUMBER] adults, with an average wait of [X] months from intake to tutor match. Evening and weekend slots, which working parents most need, fill within [X] days of opening.

What residents describe is as clear as any statistic. "I've been hiding this my whole life. I want to read to my daughter before she figures out I can't," one prospective learner told our intake coordinator in [MONTH YEAR]. Another, a [City] resident on our waitlist for [X] months, said simply: "I just need someone to give me a chance to start."

Funding now will allow us to clear our waitlist within [X] months, expand evening tutoring capacity by [X]%, and reach an additional [NUMBER] adults over the grant period. The need in [City] is not abstract; it is sitting on a waitlist, working a shift that doesn't pay enough, and waiting for a chance to begin. With this investment, [Organization] can meet that moment with the trained tutors, materials, and wraparound supports our neighbors are already asking for.

---

## Three Specific Sources to Pull

**`[CITE #1]` — National/local literacy rate statistic (opener and paragraph 2)**
→ **PIAAC State and County Estimates of Adult Literacy and Numeracy**, U.S. Department of Education, National Center for Education Statistics (NCES). This is the standard source for county-level adult literacy rates in the U.S. Pull the most recent estimates for your county and state. URL: nces.ed.gov/surveys/piaac/skillsmap

**`[CITE #2]` — Educational attainment and trend data (paragraphs 2 and 3)**
→ **U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey (ACS) 5-Year Estimates, Table S1501 "Educational Attainment."** Pull your city, county, and state data for the most recent year and compare with the 2013–2017 or 2014–2018 estimates to show the trend. Available via data.census.gov.

**`[CITE #3]` — State adult education enrollment and gap data (paragraph 2)**
→ **National Reporting System (NRS) for Adult Education, state-level enrollment reports**, published annually by your state's Department of Education / Office of Adult Education. These show how many eligible adults are served vs. the total eligible population by county. Search "[State] adult education annual performance report" or check nrsweb.org for the state data tables.

**Bonus (strengthens paragraph 3):** Your [Regional Workforce Board]'s most recent **Comprehensive Economic Development Strategy (CEDS)** or labor market information (LMI) report, usually posted on the workforce board's site. These give you the skill-demand projection that connects literacy to local jobs — a hook funders respond to.

## Program Design & Activities

[Organization]'s program is designed around a simple premise supported by three decades of adult education research: low-literacy adults make durable gains when instruction is individualized, delivered consistently over time, and connected to the real-life contexts in which they want to use their skills — work, parenting, health, and civic life `[CITE #1]`. Our three core activities — one-on-one volunteer tutoring, small-group skills workshops, and monthly family literacy nights — are mutually reinforcing components of a single learner pathway, not standalone services.

**Logic model summary.** Our theory of change moves from inputs (trained volunteer tutors, credentialed staff, evidence-based curricula, partner referrals) through activities (tutoring, workshops, family nights) to outputs (hours of instruction, learners served, sessions delivered) and finally to outcomes (measurable gains in reading level, writing, and digital skills; increased parent engagement in children's learning; progression to GED prep, employment, or further education). Each activity addresses a specific barrier identified in our Statement of Need: tutoring addresses the shortage of individualized instruction, workshops build functional skills tied to local labor-market demand, and family nights address the two-generation nature of low literacy in [City].

**Participant pathway.** All learners enter through a single intake process to ensure the right fit and a clear plan. *Intake (Week 1–2):* Prospective learners complete a 60-minute intake with our Learner Services Coordinator, including the [TABE or CASAS] assessment to establish a baseline reading level, a goal-setting conversation, and a schedule match. *Services (Months 1–9):* Each learner is enrolled in at least one core activity and, where appropriate, combines tutoring with workshops or family nights. Progress is reviewed at 90-day intervals using the same assessment tool, and learning plans are updated with the tutor and learner together. *Exit and follow-up (Month 9–12):* Learners complete an exit assessment, a goal-review conversation, and a warm handoff to a next step — GED preparation at [Community College], workforce training through the [Regional Workforce Board], or continued tutoring at a higher level. We follow up at 6 and 12 months post-exit to track retention of gains and progress toward the goals learners set at intake.

**Activity 1: One-on-One Volunteer Tutoring.** Each learner is matched with a trained volunteer tutor for 2 hours per week over a minimum 9-month cycle, totaling approximately 70 hours of instruction — a dosage consistent with the threshold research associates with measurable reading-level gains in adult learners `[CITE #2]`. Tutors complete a 12-hour pre-service training based on the [Pro Literacy / LINCS] curriculum, are supported by a 0.6 FTE Tutor Coordinator (certified in adult education), and attend quarterly in-service sessions. Pairs meet at partner sites — the [City] Public Library, [Community Center], and two faith-based partners — that are geographically distributed across our highest-need ZIP codes. *Link to rubric outcomes:* This activity is the primary driver of our measurable reading-level gain outcome, as tracked through pre/post [TABE or CASAS] scores.

**Activity 2: Small-Group Skills Workshops.** Workshops run in 6-week cycles, with cohorts of 6–10 learners meeting twice weekly for 90 minutes. Three tracks are offered on a rotating basis: reading comprehension, functional writing (job applications, workplace communication, forms), and digital literacy (email, online job search, basic office software, accessing health and benefits portals). The digital literacy track directly responds to the [Regional Workforce Board]'s finding that nearly all entry-level positions in [City]'s growing sectors now require basic digital skills. Workshops are led by our 0.8 FTE Lead Instructor and an adjunct instructor, both with adult education credentials. *Link to rubric outcomes:* Workshops drive our functional-skills gain and workforce-readiness outcomes, measured by task-based pre/post assessments and learner-reported application of skills at 90 days.

**Activity 3: Monthly Family Literacy Nights.** On the second Thursday of each month, we host a 2-hour family literacy night serving approximately 20 families. Caregivers participate in a coaching session on supporting children's reading at home — drawing on evidence-based family literacy practices `[CITE #3]` — while trained volunteers lead age-appropriate literacy activities for children ages 3–12. Families leave with a free book and a take-home activity. This activity is co-designed with [City Public Library] and [Elementary School District] partners who provide space, childcare support, and book donations. *Link to rubric outcomes:* Family nights drive our parent-engagement outcome, measured by a validated home literacy practices survey administered at first attendance and again at 6 months.

Together, these activities form a coherent pathway: individualized instruction builds the foundation, workshops translate foundational skills into functional ones, and family nights extend learning into the home and the next generation. Each is staffed, dosed, and sequenced to produce the outcomes we commit to measuring in Section 7.

---

## Three Specific Sources to Pull

**`[CITE #1]` — Evidence base for individualized, contextualized adult literacy instruction (opener)**
→ **"Improving Adult Literacy Instruction: Options for Practice and Research,"** National Research Council / National Academies Press (2012), or the more recent **LINCS (Literacy Information and Communication System)** evidence-based practice briefs from the U.S. Department of Education, Office of Career, Technical, and Adult Education. URL: lincs.ed.gov. These are the standard citations for "what works" in adult literacy and are well-regarded by funders.

**`[CITE #2]` — Instructional dosage and reading-level gains (Activity 1)**
→ **Comings, J. "Persistence: Helping Adult Education Students Reach Their Goals,"** Review of Adult Learning and Literacy, Vol. 7, National Center for the Study of Adult Learning and Literacy (NCSALL). Comings' research is the most-cited source on the 70–100 hour threshold for measurable adult reading gains. Alternatively, cite **ProLiteracy's "The Impact of Adult Literacy"** research summary (proliteracy.org/resources).

**`[CITE #3]` — Family literacy evidence base (Activity 3)**
→ **National Center for Families Learning (NCFL)** research briefs, particularly those on two-generation family literacy outcomes, available at familieslearning.org. Alternatively, cite the **Barbara Bush Foundation for Family Literacy** research reports, or the U.S. Department of Education's evidence review of family literacy programs through the What Works Clearinghouse (ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc).

## Outcomes & Objectives

[Organization] commits to four measurable outcomes over the 12-month grant period, each tied directly to an activity described in Section 4 and to the needs documented in Section 2. Baselines will be established for every enrolled learner at intake using validated assessment tools, and progress will be measured at 90-day intervals by our Data & Evaluation Specialist, in place from Month 1. All outcomes distinguish between outputs (services delivered) and outcomes (measurable change in learners and families), and all targets reflect realistic gains supported by adult literacy research.

**Objective 1: Reading-level gains (primary outcome).** By Month 12, at least 180 adult learners enrolled in one-on-one tutoring will increase their reading level by a minimum of one grade-level equivalent, as measured by pre/post [TABE or CASAS] assessments administered at intake and at the 9-month exit point. This represents 60% of the 300 learners we expect to enroll over the grant period. *Baseline:* Each learner's intake score serves as their individual baseline; no learner carries a historical baseline, so Month 1–3 intakes will establish the program-wide starting profile. *Measurement:* Standardized [TABE or CASAS] administration by the Data & Evaluation Specialist, with inter-rater reliability checks.

**Objective 2: Functional and digital skills gains.** By Month 12, at least 75% of learners completing a 6-week workshop cycle will demonstrate measurable improvement on a task-based pre/post assessment aligned to the workshop track (reading comprehension, functional writing, or digital literacy). *Baseline:* Pre-cycle task assessment administered in Week 1 of each cycle. *Measurement:* Rubric-scored task performance plus learner self-report at 90 days post-cycle on application of skills in work, parenting, or daily life.

**Objective 3: Family literacy engagement.** By Month 12, at least 60 caregivers attending two or more Family Literacy Nights will report increased frequency and quality of home literacy practices with their children, as measured by a validated home literacy practices survey administered at first attendance and again at 6 months. Target: a statistically meaningful increase on the survey's composite score for at least 70% of repeat attendees. *Baseline:* First-attendance survey score.

**Objective 4: Progression to next-step pathways.** By Month 12, at least 40% of learners exiting the program (approximately 72 learners from the first cohort) will be enrolled in or have completed a next step — GED preparation, workforce training, employment, or continued higher-level tutoring — tracked at exit and at 6-month follow-up. *Baseline:* Learner-reported goal and status at intake. *Measurement:* Exit interview and follow-up contact by the Learner Services Coordinator.

Together, these four outcomes capture both the depth (skill gains) and the reach (family and pathway effects) of the program, and each is directly measurable with the tools and staffing described in Sections 5 and 7.

## Evaluation Plan

[Organization]'s evaluation is designed to answer three questions for the funder and for ourselves: Are learners making measurable skill gains? Are family and pathway outcomes following? And what should we adjust to serve learners better? The plan uses a pre/post design with a matched comparison element, standardized instruments, and a quarterly feedback loop that makes evaluation a program-improvement tool, not just a reporting requirement.

**Design.** The primary design is a within-learner pre/post comparison using validated assessments at intake, 90 days, 180 days, and exit (approximately 9 months). For the reading-level outcome (Objective 1), we will add a quasi-experimental comparison: tutoring-pair learners (treatment) will be compared to workshop-only learners with similar intake profiles (comparison), matched on baseline reading level, age band, and primary language. This allows us to estimate the added effect of individualized tutoring beyond workshop participation. We will also track 6-month post-exit outcomes to assess retention of gains.

**Instruments and frequency.** Instruments include: [TABE or CASAS] reading assessment (intake, 90 days, exit, 6-month follow-up); workshop task-based rubric assessments (Week 1 and Week 6 of each cycle); home literacy practices survey (first family night, 6 months); learner goal-and-pathway interview (intake, exit, 6-month follow-up); and brief tutor/instructor session logs capturing dosage and content (every session). Learner satisfaction surveys will be administered at 90 days and exit.

**Analytic methods.** The Data & Evaluation Specialist (0.4 FTE, in place Month 1) will lead analyses, with quarterly review by the Program Director. Quantitative analyses include paired t-tests and effect-size calculations for pre/post gains, descriptive statistics for output measures, and matched-group comparison for the tutoring vs. workshop-only analysis. Qualitative data from exit interviews will be coded thematically to surface learner-reported barriers and successes.

**Privacy and consent.** All learners complete a plain-language informed consent at intake, available in English and [second language], covering data collection, use, storage, and the right to withdraw without losing services. Data is stored in a password-protected, access-controlled database ([LACES or equivalent adult education data system]), with personally identifiable information separated from analytic datasets. All staff complete annual data-privacy training.

**Reporting cadence.** Internal dashboards will be updated monthly and reviewed in quarterly program meetings to inform real-time adjustments. We will deliver a midterm narrative and data report to the funder in Month 7, a final evaluation report in Month 12, and a 6-month post-grant follow-up summary. Findings will also be shared with partners and, in aggregate form, with the learners themselves.

---

LACES is free in many states through the state adult ed office — worth confirming before budgeting a data system line. The external evaluation consultant is optional but often strengthens credibility with funders; if you include it, name the consultant or firm in the budget justification.
